6-6-8.title: Das, Kar & Parrila
6-6-8.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Das, Kar and Parrila are associated with the PASS framework of cognitive processing: Planning, Attention–Arousal, Simultaneous processing and Successive processing. Baron & Misra explain that planning involves goal setting and monitoring, attention involves selective attention and vigilance, simultaneous processing integrates stimuli into wholes, and successive processing integrates information in a specific serial order.

KEY POINTS
• P = Planning: goal setting, problem solving and monitoring.
• A = Attention/Arousal: selective attention, resistance to distraction and vigilance.
• S = Simultaneous: integrates elements into a whole.
• S = Successive: integrates elements in a serial order.

SOURCE BASIS
Baron & Misra — PASS Theory of Intelligence (Das, Naglieri & Kirby); PowerWithin Psychology — Das, Kar & Parrila.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
PASS describes cognitive processes rather than reducing intelligence to one general score.

MEMORY CUE
Das, Kar & Parrila → P = Planning: goal setting, problem solving and monitoring • A = Attention/Arousal: selective attention, resistance to distraction and vigilance • S = Simultaneous: integrates elements into a whole

6-7-2.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Getzels and Jackson are associated with research examining the relationship between creativity and intelligence. The uploaded PowerWithin material describes comparisons between students identified through creativity tests and intelligence measures, illustrating that high creativity and high intelligence need not be identical groupings.

KEY POINTS
• Creativity and intelligence can be distinguished conceptually.
• Getzels and Jackson compared groups using creativity and intelligence measures.
• Their work is relevant to the debate about whether creativity is reducible to intelligence.
• The source places their work within creativity theory/testing.

SOURCE BASIS

6-7-3.title: Guilford
6-7-3.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Guilford developed a major framework for creativity and proposed the Structure of Intellect model. The uploaded PowerWithin material describes intellectual operations, contents and products, with divergent production among the operations. Creativity is associated with generating varied and original possibilities.

KEY POINTS
• Guilford emphasized divergent production.
• His Structure of Intellect model organizes abilities by operations, contents and products.
• Divergent production concerns generating multiple possibilities.
• Fluency, flexibility and originality are central creativity-related abilities in the source tradition.

Divergent production is not the same as convergent production, which focuses on arriving at a single appropriate answer.

6-8-1.title: Relationship between intelligence and creativity
6-8-1.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
The uploaded sources treat intelligence and creativity as related but distinguishable constructs. Baron & Misra's confluence approach describes creativity as emerging from the convergence of intellectual abilities, thinking styles, personality traits, supportive environments, intrinsic motivation and knowledge. Their cited evidence found intellectual ability, thinking style and personality related to creativity, while creativity across domains was only moderately related.

KEY POINTS
• Intelligence can contribute to creativity but is not sufficient by itself.
• Creativity involves multiple interacting conditions.
• Domain knowledge and intrinsic motivation can support creative performance.
• Creativity can vary across domains.

SOURCE BASIS
Baron & Misra — Creativity: A Confluence Approach; PowerWithin Psychology — Relationship between Intelligence and Creativity.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Do not reduce creativity to IQ; the source explicitly presents a multi-factor/confluence account.

MEMORY CUE
Relationship between intelligence and creativity → Intelligence can contribute to creativity but is not sufficient by itself • Creativity involves multiple interacting conditions • Domain knowledge and intrinsic motivation can support creative performance

7-1-1.title: Biological determinants
7-1-1.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Biological determinants of personality include inherited characteristics, nervous-system processes and other biological factors that contribute to individual differences. The uploaded sources discuss behavioral genetics and the biology of personality while emphasizing interaction with environmental experience.

KEY POINTS
• Genes contribute to individual differences.
• Biological systems can influence temperament and behavior.
• Twin/adoption evidence is relevant to behavioral-genetic questions.
• Biological influence does not imply complete determinism.

SOURCE BASIS
Ciccarelli & White 6e — Biology of Personality and Behavioral Genetics; Baron & Misra.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Biological determinants are one part of personality explanation; they do not exclude learning, culture or social experience.

7-2-1.title: Psychoanalytical approach
7-2-1.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
The psychoanalytic approach explains personality through unconscious processes, internal conflict and developmental experiences. Ciccarelli & White describe Freud's id, ego and superego, with the ego managing conflicts between impulses and moral restrictions and using defense mechanisms to reduce anxiety.

KEY POINTS
• Freud proposed conscious, preconscious and unconscious processes.
• Id follows the pleasure principle.
• Ego follows the reality principle.
• Superego represents moral standards; defense mechanisms manage anxiety.

SOURCE BASIS
Ciccarelli & White 6e — Psychodynamic Perspectives; Baron & Misra — Psychoanalytic approach.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Psychoanalytic explanations emphasize unconscious conflict and development, unlike trait approaches that focus on measurable patterns of characteristics.

MEMORY CUE
Psychoanalytical approach → Freud proposed conscious, preconscious and unconscious processes • Id follows the pleasure principle • Ego follows the reality principle

7-2-3.title: Social learning approach
7-2-3.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
The social learning approach explains personality through learned behavior and the influence of social models, reinforcement and expectations. The uploaded sources connect personality with behavioral and social-cognitive learning processes rather than treating traits as completely independent of experience.

KEY POINTS
• Behavior can be learned through observation and consequences.
• Social context influences behavior.
• Expectations and perceived consequences affect action.
• Personality can reflect learned patterns rather than fixed traits alone.

SOURCE BASIS
Ciccarelli & White 6e — Behavioral and Social Cognitive View of Personality; Baron & Misra.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Social learning is broader than simple conditioning because observational and cognitive processes also matter.

MEMORY CUE

7-2-4.title: Trait and Type approach
7-2-4.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Trait and type approaches describe relatively stable patterns of characteristics that distinguish individuals. Baron & Misra define personality as unique and relatively stable patterns of behavior, thoughts and emotions, while trait theories measure dimensions such as characteristic tendencies.

KEY POINTS
• Traits are relatively stable characteristics.
• Type approaches classify people into broader categories.
• Trait approaches allow dimensions and degrees of a characteristic.
• Measurement and consistency across situations are important issues.

SOURCE BASIS
Baron & Misra — Personality: Individuals, Unique and Relatively Stable Patterns; Ciccarelli & White — Trait Theories.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Trait stability is not absolute; Baron & Misra discuss the debate over person–situation consistency.

MEMORY CUE
Trait and Type approach → Traits are relatively stable characteristics • Type approaches classify people into broader categories • Trait approaches allow dimensions and degrees of a characteristic

7-2-5.title: Cognitive approach
7-2-5.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
The cognitive approach emphasizes how people interpret events, form beliefs and expectations, and use mental representations in shaping behavior. Personality is therefore linked to characteristic ways of thinking and interpreting social situations.

KEY POINTS
• Interpretation of events influences behavior.
• Expectancies and beliefs affect action.
• Cognitive patterns can show individual differences.
• Personality is understood partly through information processing and meaning-making.

SOURCE BASIS
Ciccarelli & White 6e — Behavioral/Social Cognitive and Cognitive influences on Personality; PowerWithin Psychology.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
The cognitive approach is not the same as the information-processing account of basic perception; here the focus is personality-related cognition.

MEMORY CUE
Cognitive approach → Interpretation of events influences behavior • Expectancies and beliefs affect action • Cognitive patterns can show individual differences

7-3-2.title: Seligman's Explanatory styles
7-3-2.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Seligman's explanatory-style framework concerns habitual ways of explaining positive and negative events. The broader optimism literature in the uploaded sources contrasts optimistic and pessimistic patterns in how people explain outcomes, with implications for persistence and coping.

KEY POINTS
• Explanations can differ in how permanent or temporary an outcome is seen.
• Explanations can differ in how broadly an event is generalized.
• Explanatory style is linked to expectations and coping.
• The framework is relevant to learned optimism and pessimism.

PowerWithin Psychology — Seligman/optimism material; Ciccarelli & White on optimism and stress.

Explanatory style concerns habitual interpretation of events; it is not identical to a global personality trait score.

7-4-1.title: Instincts
7-4-1.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Instincts are innate behavior patterns or predispositions that do not depend on prior learning. The uploaded Self-Teaching Guide distinguishes biological drives from acquired motives and places instinct concepts within historical explanations of motivation.

KEY POINTS
• Instincts are biologically based.
• They do not require the same kind of learning as acquired motives.
• Evolutionary explanations can be used to understand adaptive behavior.
• Human motivation is not explained by instincts alone in modern psychology.

SOURCE BASIS
Psychology: A Self-Teaching Guide — Motivation; PowerWithin Psychology — Approaches to Motivation.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Instinct and drive are related biological concepts but are not interchangeable: a drive is a motivational state, while an instinct refers to an innate behavioral tendency.

MEMORY CUE
Instincts → Instincts are biologically based • They do not require the same kind of learning as acquired motives • Evolutionary explanations can be used to understand adaptive behavior

7-4-2.title: Needs
7-4-2.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Needs are conditions or requirements that motivate behavior toward maintaining the organism or achieving psychological goals. The uploaded sources distinguish physiological needs from psychological or acquired motives and discuss needs in motivational theories.

KEY POINTS
• Physiological needs include states such as hunger and thirst.
• Psychological needs can involve achievement, affiliation or power.
• Needs can activate goal-directed behavior.
• Different theories organize needs differently.

SOURCE BASIS
Self-Teaching Guide — Motivation and Biological/Acquired Motives; Ciccarelli & White — Motivation.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
A need is not identical to a drive: a need refers to a requirement or deficiency, whereas a drive is the motivational state that can arise from it.

MEMORY CUE
Needs → Physiological needs include states such as hunger and thirst • Psychological needs can involve achievement, affiliation or power • Needs can activate goal-directed behavior

7-4-3.title: Drives
7-4-3.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
A drive is a motivational state associated with physiological or psychological arousal that directs behavior. The Self-Teaching Guide defines a motive as a state of physiological or psychological arousal that can play a causal role in behavior and discusses biological drives such as hunger and thirst.

KEY POINTS
• Drives can arise from physiological states.
• Drive reduction theory links motivation with restoring homeostasis.
• Drives energize and direct behavior.
• Psychological motives can also influence behavior.

SOURCE BASIS
Psychology: A Self-Teaching Guide — Motivation; Ciccarelli & White — Drive-Reduction Theory.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Drive is not the same as incentive: a drive originates in an internal motivational state, whereas an incentive is an external or learned attraction/reward.

MEMORY CUE
Drives → Drives can arise from physiological states • Drive reduction theory links motivation with restoring homeostasis • Drives energize and direct behavior

7-4-4.title: Arousal
7-4-4.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Arousal refers to a level of physiological or psychological activation. Ciccarelli & White describe arousal theory as the idea that people seek an optimal level of stimulation, sometimes increasing stimulation when underaroused and reducing it when overaroused.

KEY POINTS
• People may seek an optimal level of stimulation.
• Underarousal can motivate exploration or stimulation.
• Overarousal can motivate reduction of stimulation.
• Individual differences occur in desired arousal levels.

SOURCE BASIS
Ciccarelli & White 6e — Arousal Theory; PowerWithin Psychology — Motivation.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Arousal theory differs from drive reduction: it concerns an optimal level of stimulation rather than simply correcting a physiological deficit.

MEMORY CUE
Arousal → People may seek an optimal level of stimulation • Underarousal can motivate exploration or stimulation • Overarousal can motivate reduction of stimulation

7-4-5.title: Incentives
7-4-5.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Incentives are external or learned rewards that attract behavior. Ciccarelli & White describe incentive approaches as explaining behavior through anticipated rewards, such as eating a desirable food even when hunger is not strong.

KEY POINTS
• Incentives can attract behavior.
• They may be learned rather than biologically necessary.
• The same incentive can have different value for different people.
• Incentives complement internal motivational states.

SOURCE BASIS
Ciccarelli & White 6e — Incentive Approach; Self-Teaching Guide — acquired motives.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
An incentive is not the same as a drive; incentives are external/learned attractions, whereas drives involve internal motivational states.

MEMORY CUE
Incentives → Incentives can attract behavior • They may be learned rather than biologically necessary • The same incentive can have different value for different people

7-4-6.title: Motivational cycle
7-4-6.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
The motivational cycle describes how a need or motivational state creates tension, directs behavior toward a goal, and is reduced or transformed when the goal is reached. The Self-Teaching Guide links motivation with internal physiological or psychological arousal that influences action.

KEY POINTS
• A need or motive initiates motivational activity.
• Arousal energizes goal-directed behavior.
• Behavior is directed toward an objective or incentive.
• Goal attainment can reduce or change the motivational state.

SOURCE BASIS
Self-Teaching Guide — Motivation; PowerWithin Psychology — Basic Motivational Concepts.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
The cycle is a conceptual model; not every human motive follows a simple linear sequence.

MEMORY CUE
Motivational cycle → A need or motive initiates motivational activity • Arousal energizes goal-directed behavior • Behavior is directed toward an objective or incentive

7-5-1.title: Psychoanalytical approach
7-5-1.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
The psychoanalytic approach explains motivation through unconscious wishes, conflicts and instinctual energies. The Self-Teaching Guide and personality material place biological and unconscious motives within the psychodynamic tradition.

KEY POINTS
• Unconscious motives can influence behavior.
• Instinctual drives are central in Freud's model.
• Conflict can create motivational tension.
• Behavior may express motives indirectly.

SOURCE BASIS
Self-Teaching Guide — Unconscious Motives and Psychoanalytic Theory; PowerWithin Psychology.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Psychoanalytic motivation is not equivalent to conscious goal setting; unconscious processes are central to the approach.

MEMORY CUE
Psychoanalytical approach → Unconscious motives can influence behavior • Instinctual drives are central in Freud's model • Conflict can create motivational tension

7-5-2.title: Ethological approach
7-5-2.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
The ethological approach explains motivation in relation to evolved behavior patterns and their adaptive value. It emphasizes behavior that has been shaped by natural selection and the species-specific conditions under which it is expressed.

KEY POINTS
• Behavior can have evolutionary functions.
• Innate tendencies are considered in relation to environmental conditions.
• The approach emphasizes adaptation and species-typical behavior.
• It differs from purely learned accounts of motivation.

SOURCE BASIS
PowerWithin Psychology — Ethological Approach to Motivation; evolutionary/biological material in Baron & Misra.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
An evolutionary explanation is not a claim that every behavior is fixed; behavior can still be influenced by learning and context.

MEMORY CUE
Ethological approach → Behavior can have evolutionary functions • Innate tendencies are considered in relation to environmental conditions • The approach emphasizes adaptation and species-typical behavior

7-5-3.title: S-R Cognitive approach
7-5-3.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
The S-R cognitive approach connects motivation with the relationship between environmental situations, internal cognitive processes and behavioral responses. The cognitive emphasis recognizes that people interpret situations and expectations rather than responding mechanically to stimuli.

KEY POINTS
• Stimulus conditions can influence behavior.
• Cognitive interpretation mediates responses.
• Expectancies and goals can influence motivated action.
• The approach goes beyond a simple stimulus-response chain.

SOURCE BASIS
PowerWithin Psychology — S-R Cognitive Approach to Motivation; cognitive approaches to motivation.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
The cognitive component is essential; do not reduce this approach to simple behaviorism.

MEMORY CUE
S-R Cognitive approach → Stimulus conditions can influence behavior • Cognitive interpretation mediates responses • Expectancies and goals can influence motivated action

7-5-4.title: Humanistic approach
7-5-4.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
The humanistic approach views people as active agents motivated toward growth, self-development and fulfillment. The Self-Teaching Guide discusses self-actualization as a central humanistic motive, while Ciccarelli & White discusses psychological needs and intrinsic motivation.

KEY POINTS
• Growth and self-actualization are central.
• Motivation includes psychological as well as biological needs.
• Intrinsic motivation can arise from interest and mastery.
• The person is treated as an active agent rather than a passive responder.

SOURCE BASIS
Self-Teaching Guide — Self-Actualization; Ciccarelli & White — Humanistic Motivation.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Humanistic motivation differs from drive reduction because the goal is not simply restoration of physiological balance.

MEMORY CUE
Humanistic approach → Growth and self-actualization are central • Motivation includes psychological as well as biological needs • Intrinsic motivation can arise from interest and mastery

7-6-1.title: Exploratory behavior
7-6-1.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Exploratory behavior involves seeking information, stimulation or environmental novelty. Ciccarelli & White places exploration among stimulus motives and notes that such behavior can occur without a clear biological deficit.

KEY POINTS
• Exploration can increase stimulation or information.
• It can occur without deprivation of a basic physiological need.
• Novelty and curiosity can energize behavior.
• Exploration has adaptive and learning-related value.

SOURCE BASIS
Ciccarelli & White 6e — Arousal and Incentive Approaches; PowerWithin Psychology — Exploratory Behaviour.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Exploratory behavior is not necessarily goal-free; it can serve information gathering and environmental mastery.

MEMORY CUE
Exploratory behavior → Exploration can increase stimulation or information • It can occur without deprivation of a basic physiological need • Novelty and curiosity can energize behavior

7-6-2.title: Curiosity

Curiosity is a motive to seek information, novelty or understanding. Ciccarelli & White treats curiosity as an example of a stimulus motive, while the NET material places it with exploratory behavior.

• Curiosity can motivate information seeking.
• It can be triggered by novelty or uncertainty.
• Curiosity can support learning and exploration.
• It can occur even without a physiological deficit.

SOURCE BASIS
Ciccarelli & White 6e — Stimulus Motives; PowerWithin Psychology — Curiosity.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Curiosity is a motivational process, not simply a personality label.

MEMORY CUE
Curiosity → Curiosity can motivate information seeking • It can be triggered by novelty or uncertainty • Curiosity can support learning and exploration

7-7-1.title: Zuckerman’s Sensation seeking
7-7-1.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Zuckerman's sensation-seeking construct concerns individual differences in the need for stimulation and novel or intense experiences. Ciccarelli & White describes sensation seekers as people who seek higher levels of arousal than average.

KEY POINTS
• Sensation seeking reflects a preference for stimulation.
• People differ in their desired arousal levels.
• Novel or intense activities can satisfy higher stimulation needs.
• The construct is linked with arousal theory.

SOURCE BASIS
Ciccarelli & White 6e — Arousal Theory and Zuckerman's Sensation Seeking; Baron & Misra.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Sensation seeking is an individual-difference construct, not simply a synonym for risk-taking; risk may be one possible expression.

MEMORY CUE
Zuckerman’s Sensation seeking → Sensation seeking reflects a preference for stimulation • People differ in their desired arousal levels • Novel or intense activities can satisfy higher stimulation needs

7-10-1.title: Self-regulation
7-10-1.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Self-regulation involves monitoring and controlling one's thoughts, emotions and behavior in relation to goals. The uploaded sources connect self-regulation with metacognition, motivation and behavior change.

KEY POINTS
• Goals provide standards for regulation.
• Monitoring tracks progress and internal states.
• Regulation can involve changing strategies or behavior.
• Self-regulation supports persistence and goal pursuit.

SOURCE BASIS
PowerWithin Psychology — Self-Regulation; REVISATHON Part 1 — Metacognitive Regulation; Ciccarelli & White.

COMMON EXAM TRAP

• The autonomic nervous system contributes to bodily changes.
• Brain structures such as the amygdala are involved in emotional processing.
• Different theories assign different causal roles to physiological arousal.

Physiological arousal is one component of emotion, not a complete definition of emotion.

7-13-4.title: Lazarus theory
7-13-4.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Lazarus's cognitive-mediational theory proposes that cognitive appraisal of a situation is central to emotional experience. The uploaded sources state that appraisal mediates between the stimulus and the emotional response; a situation judged threatening can elicit action tendencies and physiological responses, while reappraisal can alter the response.

KEY POINTS
• Appraisal is central to emotion.
• The interpretation of the stimulus comes before the emotional response in the model.
• Primary appraisal concerns significance/threat; secondary appraisal concerns coping resources/options.
• Reappraisal can change how a situation is experienced.

SOURCE BASIS
Ciccarelli & White 6e — Lazarus's Cognitive-Mediational Theory; PowerWithin Psychology — Lazarus Theory.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Lazarus's theory is cognitive-mediational; it differs from James–Lange and Cannon–Bard in the proposed role and timing of appraisal.

MEMORY CUE
Lazarus theory → Appraisal is central to emotion • The interpretation of the stimulus comes before the emotional response in the model • Primary appraisal concerns significance/threat; secondary appraisal concerns coping resources/options

7-15-2.title: Types of conflict
7-15-2.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
The uploaded Self-Teaching Guide distinguishes approach–approach, avoidance–avoidance, approach–avoidance and double/multiple approach–avoidance conflicts. The classification depends on whether alternatives are attractive, unattractive or mixed.

KEY POINTS
• Approach–approach: choose between two desirable alternatives.
• Avoidance–avoidance: choose between two undesirable alternatives.
• Approach–avoidance: one goal has both positive and negative features.
• Double approach–avoidance: multiple alternatives each have positive and negative features.

7-16-2.title: Models of stress and coping
7-16-2.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
The uploaded sources present stress through physiological, psychological and cognitive-appraisal models. Ciccarelli & White describes stress as depending partly on appraisal of demands and coping resources, while Lazarus's approach distinguishes appraisal of the event from appraisal of coping options.

KEY POINTS
• Stress depends on both demands and appraisal.
• Cognitive appraisal influences whether an event is experienced as stressful.
• Coping can be problem-focused or emotion-focused.
• Reappraisal can change the experience of a stressor.

SOURCE BASIS
Ciccarelli & White 6e — Stress and Health; PowerWithin Psychology — Stress and Coping.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
A stressor is the event or demand; stress is the psychological/physiological response to it.

7-16-3.title: Type A behavior
7-16-3.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Type A behavior is a cluster including competitiveness, impatience and hostility. Baron & Misra describe the original observations of Friedman and Rosenman and later evidence linking cynical hostility particularly strongly with cardiovascular risk.

KEY POINTS
• Competitiveness is a characteristic of the pattern.
• Impatience and time urgency are common features.
• Hostility is especially relevant in the health literature discussed by Baron & Misra.
• The pattern can be modified through behavior change.

SOURCE BASIS
Baron & Misra — Type A Behavior Pattern; Ciccarelli & White — Personality and Stress.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Type A is a behavior pattern, not a diagnosis; the source specifically discusses components rather than treating the label as a single cause of disease.

MEMORY CUE
Type A behavior → Competitiveness is a characteristic of the pattern • Impatience and time urgency are common features • Hostility is especially relevant in the health literature discussed by Baron & Misra

7-17-1.title: Biofeedback
7-17-1.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Biofeedback is a technique in which information about physiological activity is fed back to the person so that the person can learn to regulate that activity. The uploaded psychology material includes biofeedback among stress-management strategies and treats it as a way of gaining control over physiological responses.

KEY POINTS
• Physiological information is measured and fed back.
• The person learns voluntary control over a physiological response.
• It is used as a self-regulation technique.
• It differs from relaxation alone because feedback about bodily activity is central.

SOURCE BASIS
PowerWithin Psychology — Stress Management Strategies; Self-Teaching Guide/Ciccarelli & White on biofeedback.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Biofeedback is a training procedure using physiological feedback; it is not simply another name for meditation or relaxation.

MEMORY CUE
Biofeedback → Physiological information is measured and fed back • The person learns voluntary control over a physiological response • It is used as a self-regulation technique

8-1-1.title: Nature of social psychology
8-1-1.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Social psychology studies how people think about, influence and relate to other people. The uploaded NET material emphasizes the social context of behavior, while Kaplan organizes the field around social perception, attitudes, group processes and social influence.

KEY POINTS
• Social context is central to explanation.
• The field examines cognition, affect and behavior in social situations.
• Individuals and groups are both relevant levels of analysis.
• Social psychology connects individual processes with interpersonal and group contexts.

SOURCE BASIS
PowerWithin Psychology — Unit 8 What is Social Psychology?; Kaplan AP Psychology — Social Psychology.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Social psychology is not simply the study of groups; many social-psychological processes occur at the individual level in social contexts.

MEMORY CUE
Nature of social psychology → Social context is central to explanation • The field examines cognition, affect and behavior in social situations • Individuals and groups are both relevant levels of analysis

• Attitudes and their change are studied.
• Groups and social influence are major domains.
• Intergroup relations and applied social psychology extend the field.

Scope is broader than one topic such as conformity; the NET outline treats social psychology as a wide set of interacting domains.

8-2-1.title: Field theory
8-2-1.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Field theory, associated with Kurt Lewin, explains behavior as a function of the person and the psychological environment. Social behavior is therefore understood within a dynamic field of forces rather than as a property of the individual alone.

KEY POINTS
• Lewin is the key theorist.
• Behavior is considered in relation to person and environment.
• The psychological field contains interacting forces.
• The approach is dynamic and situational.

SOURCE BASIS
PowerWithin Psychology — Theoretical Perspectives in Social Psychology; Lewinian field-theory coverage.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Field theory is not simply an environmental theory; the person and environment are considered together.

MEMORY CUE
Field theory → Lewin is the key theorist • Behavior is considered in relation to person and environment • The psychological field contains interacting forces

8-2-3.title: Sociobiology
8-2-3.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Sociobiology applies evolutionary reasoning to social behavior, asking how behavioral tendencies may relate to adaptation and reproductive success. The uploaded NET material includes sociobiology as one theoretical perspective in social psychology.

KEY POINTS
• Social behavior can be examined through evolutionary principles.
• Adaptive consequences are relevant to explanation.
• The approach complements rather than replaces social and cultural explanations.
• Genetic influence does not imply fixed behavior in every context.

SOURCE BASIS
PowerWithin Psychology — Theoretical Perspectives in Social Psychology, Sociobiology.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Sociobiological explanations concern evolutionary function; they should not be treated as proof that a behavior is genetically predetermined.

MEMORY CUE
Sociobiology → Social behavior can be examined through evolutionary principles • Adaptive consequences are relevant to explanation • The approach complements rather than replaces social and cultural explanations

• Meaning depends partly on context and interpretation.
• Communication affects interpersonal relationships.
• Misinterpretation can contribute to social conflict.

Communication is the process of exchanging information; persuasion is a specific social-influence process aimed at changing attitudes or behavior.

8-3-3.title: Attributions
8-3-3.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Attribution is the process of explaining the causes of behavior. Baron & Misra discuss internal and external attributions and the self-serving bias, in which positive outcomes are more likely to be attributed internally and negative outcomes externally.

KEY POINTS
• Internal attributions locate causes in the person.
• External attributions locate causes in the situation.
• Attributions influence judgments of self and others.
• Self-serving bias can affect explanations of outcomes.

SOURCE BASIS
Baron & Misra — Attribution and Social Cognition; Kaplan AP Psychology — Attributions.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
An attribution is an explanation of cause, not merely an observation of behavior.

MEMORY CUE
Attributions → Internal attributions locate causes in the person • External attributions locate causes in the situation • Attributions influence judgments of self and others

8-3-4.title: Attitude
8-3-4.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
An attitude is an evaluative tendency toward a person, object, issue or behavior. The uploaded sources treat attitudes as important social-psychological constructs that can influence behavior and can themselves be changed by experience and persuasion.

KEY POINTS
• Attitudes have an evaluative component.
• They can be positive, negative or mixed.
• Attitudes can influence behavior under appropriate conditions.
• Attitudes are shaped by social experience and information.

SOURCE BASIS
Baron & Misra — Social Psychology; PowerWithin Psychology — Attitude and Attitude Change.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
An attitude is an evaluation, not simply knowledge or a belief; beliefs may contribute to an attitude.

MEMORY CUE
Attitude → Attitudes have an evaluative component • They can be positive, negative or mixed • Attitudes can influence behavior under appropriate conditions

8-3-5.title: Attitude change
8-3-5.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Attitude change involves modification of an existing evaluation. The uploaded sources discuss persuasion and cognitive dissonance as important mechanisms through which attitudes can change. Dissonance can arise from inconsistency between attitudes and behavior and motivate efforts to reduce the inconsistency.

KEY POINTS
• Persuasive communication can change attitudes.
• Cognitive dissonance can motivate attitude change.
• The direction and durability of change depend on context and processing.
• Attitude change is distinct from simple exposure to information.

SOURCE BASIS
Baron & Misra — Attitude Change and Cognitive Dissonance; Kaplan AP Psychology.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Cognitive dissonance is one mechanism of attitude change, not a synonym for all attitude change.

MEMORY CUE
Attitude change → Persuasive communication can change attitudes • Cognitive dissonance can motivate attitude change • The direction and durability of change depend on context and processing

8-3-6.title: Cultural context of attitudes
8-3-6.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Attitudes develop and operate within cultural contexts that shape norms, values, social roles and interpretation. The uploaded NET material explicitly places attitude change within cultural context, and Baron & Misra repeatedly discuss cultural influences on social behavior.

KEY POINTS
• Culture provides norms and values relevant to evaluation.
• The same behavior can be evaluated differently across cultural contexts.
• Attitude expression is influenced by social expectations.
• Cross-cultural interpretation requires attention to context.

SOURCE BASIS
PowerWithin Psychology — Attitude and Cultural Context; Baron & Misra — culture and social behavior.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Cultural context influences attitudes but does not make every individual within a culture identical.

MEMORY CUE
Cultural context of attitudes → Culture provides norms and values relevant to evaluation • The same behavior can be evaluated differently across cultural contexts • Attitude expression is influenced by social expectations

8-3-7.title: Prosocial behavior
8-3-7.content_notes:

Prosocial behavior refers to actions intended to benefit other people. Kaplan describes prosocial behavior as behavior that benefits others, while the sources discuss helping, altruism, empathy and social factors that influence helping.

• Helping and altruism are common examples.
• Empathy and social context can influence prosocial behavior.
• Costs and benefits can affect helping decisions.

Prosocial behavior is broader than altruism; altruism usually emphasizes helping without direct self-benefit.

MEMORY CUE
Prosocial behavior → The intended outcome benefits another person • Helping and altruism are common examples • Empathy and social context can influence prosocial behavior

8-4-1.title: Social Facilitation
8-4-1.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Social facilitation concerns changes in performance caused by the presence of other people. The classic pattern is that the presence of others can improve performance on well-learned or simple tasks but impair performance on difficult or unfamiliar tasks.

KEY POINTS
• Audience presence can affect performance.
• Well-learned tasks may show improved performance.
• Difficult or novel tasks can show impaired performance.
• The effect is distinct from social loafing, which concerns reduced effort in groups.

SOURCE BASIS
Kaplan AP Psychology — Social Facilitation; Baron & Misra — Social Facilitation.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Social facilitation is about performance in the presence of others; social loafing is about effort in group tasks.

MEMORY CUE
Social Facilitation → Audience presence can affect performance • Well-learned tasks may show improved performance • Difficult or novel tasks can show impaired performance

8-4-2.title: Social loafing
8-4-2.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Social loafing is the tendency for individuals to exert less effort when working collectively than when working alone, particularly when individual contributions are less identifiable. Kaplan explicitly identifies larger group settings as a context in which social loafing can occur.

KEY POINTS
• Effort can decline in group tasks.
• Individual contribution may be less identifiable.
• The effect differs from social facilitation.
• Group size and accountability can influence the effect.

SOURCE BASIS
Kaplan AP Psychology — Social Loafing; PowerWithin Psychology — Group and Social Influence.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Social loafing concerns reduced effort; it is not simply any decline in performance caused by being in a group.

MEMORY CUE
Social loafing → Effort can decline in group tasks • Individual contribution may be less identifiable • The effect differs from social facilitation

8-4-4.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Peer pressure refers to influence from peers that affects a person's attitudes, choices or behavior. It can operate through explicit demands, social expectations or the desire to belong.

• Peers can influence behavior directly or indirectly.
• Conformity and group norms are related processes.
• The influence can be positive or negative depending on the behavior.
• Individual responses depend on context and perceived norms.

Peer pressure is a context of social influence; conformity is the broader process of adjusting behavior or judgments toward group norms.

MEMORY CUE

8-4-9.title: Reactance
8-4-9.content_notes:

Psychological reactance is a motivational response to perceived restriction of freedom. The uploaded social-psychology material lists reactance as a form of social influence response, and environmental material notes that perceived loss of control can increase stress reactions.

KEY POINTS
• Reactance follows perceived restriction of freedom.
• People may resist or restore the threatened choice.
• The response depends on how freedom is perceived.
• It differs from ordinary disagreement because threatened freedom is central.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Reactance is not simply stubbornness; the key condition is perceived restriction of freedom.

• Democratic leadership involves greater participation.
• Laissez-faire leadership provides greater autonomy.

A leadership style is a behavioral pattern; effectiveness depends partly on the situation rather than one style being universally effective.

8-6-3.title: Leadership effectiveness
8-6-3.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Leadership effectiveness depends on the interaction between leader characteristics, behavior and situational conditions. Revisathon material summarizes Fiedler's contingency approach: task-oriented and relationship-oriented styles may be effective depending on situational favorability.

KEY POINTS
• Leadership effectiveness is context dependent.
• Fiedler distinguishes task- and relationship-oriented styles.
• Situational favorability affects the fit between style and context.
• Other models such as path-goal theory focus on clarifying routes to goals.

SOURCE BASIS
REVISATHON Part 2 — Fiedler Contingency Approach and Path-Goal Theory.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
The contingency approach does not claim one style is always superior; it emphasizes person–situation fit.

MEMORY CUE
Leadership effectiveness → Leadership effectiveness is context dependent • Fiedler distinguishes task- and relationship-oriented styles • Situational favorability affects the fit between style and context

KEY POINTS
• Minimal categorization can create meaningful group distinctions.
• In-group favoritism can emerge with minimal group formation.
• The paradigm supports the importance of social categorization.
• It is relevant to Social Identity Theory.

SOURCE BASIS

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Minimal-group findings do not require a history of real conflict between groups; the point is that categorization itself can matter.

• People can feel deprived even when basic needs are met.
• Relative deprivation can influence group attitudes and conflict.
• The reference group or standard of comparison matters.

SOURCE BASIS

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Relative deprivation is a perception of disadvantage; it is not identical to objective poverty.

MEMORY CUE

8-8-1.title: Health applications

Applied social psychology uses knowledge about social influence, attitudes, norms and interpersonal processes to address health behavior. The uploaded NET material lists health as an application area, while Baron & Misra discuss social-psychological influences on health-related behavior.

KEY POINTS
• Health behavior is influenced by social context.
• Attitudes and norms can affect health decisions.
• Social support can influence coping and wellbeing.
• Interventions can use social-psychological principles.

Health applications are not limited to individual counseling; social norms, communication and group processes can also be intervention targets.

8-8-2.title: Environmental applications

• Crowding concerns perceived density and its psychological effects.
• Personal space regulates interpersonal distance.
• Environmental design can influence behavior.

8-8-4.title: Personal space
8-8-4.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Personal space is the preferred physical distance people maintain around themselves during social interaction. Ciccarelli & White describes it as a form of territorial protection and notes that it can be influenced by interpersonal and cultural factors.

KEY POINTS
• Personal space varies across people and situations.
• It regulates interpersonal distance.
• Crowding can occur when desired space is reduced.
• Cultural context can influence norms for interpersonal distance.

SOURCE BASIS
Ciccarelli & White 6e — Personal Space; PowerWithin Psychology — Applied Social Psychology.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Personal space is not the same as territoriality: personal space is the interpersonal distance around the person, whereas territoriality concerns control of a physical area.

MEMORY CUE
Personal space → Personal space varies across people and situations • It regulates interpersonal distance • Crowding can occur when desired space is reduced

8-8-5.title: Crowding
8-8-5.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Crowding refers to the subjective experience of having too many people or too little desired space, rather than density alone. The uploaded environmental psychology material links crowding with perceived control and stress reactions.

KEY POINTS
• Density is a physical condition; crowding is a psychological experience.
• Perceived control can influence stress responses to crowding.
• The meaning of the setting affects the experience.
• Crowding can influence interpersonal behavior and wellbeing.

SOURCE BASIS
PowerWithin Psychology — Applied Social Psychology; P2 Environment & Population Psychology — Crowding and perceived control.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
High density does not always produce crowding; crowding depends partly on perceived control and context.

MEMORY CUE
Crowding → Density is a physical condition; crowding is a psychological experience • Perceived control can influence stress responses to crowding • The meaning of the setting affects the experience

8-8-6.title: Territoriality
8-8-6.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Territoriality concerns behaviors and cognitions associated with control, ownership or defense of a physical area. The uploaded sources distinguish it from personal space and include territoriality within applied environmental social psychology.

KEY POINTS
• Territories are physical areas associated with control or ownership.
• Territorial behavior can regulate access and social interaction.
• Territoriality can occur in homes, workplaces and other settings.
• It differs from personal space because it concerns an area rather than an interpersonal radius.

SOURCE BASIS
PowerWithin Psychology — Applied Social Psychology; Ciccarelli & White — Territoriality and Personal Space.

COMMON EXAM TRAP
Territoriality is not simply the amount of personal space a person prefers.

MEMORY CUE
Territoriality → Territories are physical areas associated with control or ownership • Territorial behavior can regulate access and social interaction • Territoriality can occur in homes, workplaces and other settings

2-2-6.title: Types of variables
2-2-6.content_notes:
CORE CONCEPT
Variables are characteristics or conditions that can take different values and help structure psychological research.

KEY POINTS
• independent variable — manipulated by the researcher
• dependent variable — measured outcome
• extraneous/control variables — possible influences on the outcome that are controlled where possible
• quantitative vs qualitative
• active vs attribute
• continuous vs discrete

NET-RELEVANT TERMINOLOGY
• IV = independent variable
• DV = dependent variable
• EV = extraneous variable
• control variable = a potential influence deliberately held constant
• active variable = can be manipulated experimentally
• attribute variable = pre-existing characteristic
• continuous variable = values across a range
• discrete variable = distinct/countable values
• operational definition = specifies the measurement or manipulation procedure

COMMON CONFUSION TRAPS
• IV is not simply “the variable mentioned first”; identify its role in the design.
• DV is the measured outcome, not the presumed cause.
• An extraneous variable can become a control variable when it is deliberately held constant.
• Attribute variables are pre-existing characteristics and are not ordinarily manipulated experimentally.
• Continuous and discrete describe possible values; they are not interchangeable with IV/DV roles.

ACTIVE RECALL
1. What is the difference between an IV and a DV?
2. What makes an extraneous variable different from a control variable?
3. Distinguish active and attribute variables.
4. What is the difference between continuous and discrete variables?
5. Why is an operational definition important when studying a variable?

REVISION CUES
IV → manipulate
DV → measure

2-2-6.deep_learning:
ACADEMIC CORE
A variable is a characteristic or condition that can vary across observations. In experimental research, the independent variable is manipulated and the dependent variable is measured as the outcome.

CLASSIFICATIONS TO KNOW
1. Independent vs dependent vs extraneous/control — based on the variable's role in the research design.
2. Quantitative vs qualitative — based on the nature of the values or categories represented.
3. Active vs attribute — based on whether the variable can be experimentally manipulated.
4. Continuous vs discrete — based on the possible values the variable can take.

NET DISTINCTIONS
Independent variable → manipulated.
Dependent variable → measured.
Extraneous variable → another factor that could affect the dependent variable.
Control variable → a potential influence deliberately kept constant.
Active variable → experimentally manipulable.
Attribute variable → pre-existing characteristic.

SOURCE BASIS
• UGC NET/JRF/SLET Psychology — PowerWithin syllabus material
• Psychology: A Self-Teaching Guide
• Psychology by Ciccarelli & White (6th ed.)

STUDY RULE
Always identify a variable from its role in the particular research design. Do not assign labels mechanically from the name of the variable alone.
retrieval_questions: Without looking at the notes, define a variable and state the main research-role classifications.
In a study of the effect of sleep duration on memory performance, identify the IV and DV.
Distinguish an extraneous variable from a control variable.
How do active and attribute variables differ?
How do continuous and discrete variables differ?
2-2-6.application_question: A researcher changes room temperature and measures test performance while keeping the time of testing constant. Identify the IV, DV and control variable, and explain why each receives that label.
2-2-6.exam_takeaway: IV → manipulate | DV → measure | EV → control where possible
